blocks.text: Imagine arranging books on a shelf or selecting a team from a group. How do we count the possible ways to do this efficiently?

blocks.markdown: In many real-world problems, we need to count the number of ways to arrange or select items. These problems can often be solved using permutations and combinations, fundamental concepts in combinatorics.

blocks.title: Permutation
blocks.text: A permutation is an arrangement of items in a specific order. The order of selection matters.

blocks.title: Combination
blocks.text: A combination is a selection of items where the order does not matter.

blocks.markdown: Let's formalize these concepts. Suppose we have a set of $n$ distinct items. A permutation of $r$ items from this set is given by:

blocks.caption: Number of permutations of $r$ items from $n$ distinct items.

blocks.markdown: A combination of $r$ items from a set of $n$ distinct items is given by:

blocks.caption: Number of combinations of $r$ items from $n$ distinct items.

blocks.title: Example 1: Permutation
blocks.prompt: How many ways can 3 books be arranged on a shelf from a collection of 5 distinct books?

steps.text: Identify the problem as a permutation since the order of arrangement matters.

blocks.answer: There are 60 ways to arrange 3 books from a collection of 5.

blocks.title: Example 2: Combination
blocks.prompt: How many ways can a committee of 3 be formed from a group of 10 people?

steps.text: Identify the problem as a combination since the order of selection does not matter.

blocks.answer: There are 120 ways to form a committee of 3 from 10 people.

blocks.markdown: Permutations and combinations can also be calculated with repetition. Let's consider these cases:

blocks.title: Permutations with Repetition
blocks.text: When repetition is allowed, the number of permutations of $r$ items from $n$ distinct items is $n^r$.

blocks.title: Combinations with Repetition
blocks.text: When repetition is allowed, the number of combinations of $r$ items from $n$ distinct items is $C(n + r - 1, r)$.

points: Permutations consider order; combinations do not.
Use factorials to compute permutations and combinations.
